original_value: Primary aluminum production is an uninterrupted and complex process that must operate in a closed loop, hindering possibilities for experiments to improve production. In this sense, it is important to have ways to simulate this process computationally without acting directly on the plant, since such direct intervention could be dangerous, expensive, and time-consuming. This problem is addressed in this paper by combining real data, the artificial neural network technique, and clustering methods to create soft sensors to estimate the temperature, the aluminum fluoride percentage in the electrolytic bath, and the level of metal of aluminum reduction cells (pots). An innovative strategy is used to split the entire dataset by section and lifespan of pots with automatic clustering for soft sensors. The soft sensors created by this methodology have small estimation mean squared error with high generalization power. Results demonstrate the effectiveness and feasibility of the proposed approach to soft sensors in the aluminum industry that may improve process control and save resources.

result.paraphrase: Primary aluminum production is a continuous and intricate process that must run in a closed loop, which makes experimentation to improve production difficult. For this reason, it is important to have methods that can simulate the process computationally without direct intervention in the plant, since such intervention could be dangerous, costly, and time-consuming. This paper tackles the issue by combining real data, artificial neural networks, and clustering techniques to develop soft sensors for estimating temperature, aluminum fluoride percentage in the electrolytic bath, and the metal level of aluminum reduction cells (pots). An innovative approach splits the full dataset by pot section and lifespan using automatic clustering for the soft sensors. The resulting soft sensors show low mean squared estimation error and strong generalization ability. The results confirm the effectiveness and practicality of the proposed soft-sensor approach for the aluminum industry, with potential to improve process control and reduce resource use.
